prompt: Why does a logarithmic-space machine keep its input on a separate read-only tape?

options.text: Otherwise just storing the input would already require linear space
options.explanation: Correct. Excluding read-only input from the work-space count makes sublinear working memory meaningful.

options.text: Read-only tapes can hold only logarithmically many symbols
options.explanation: The input tape holds the whole encoded input; only the working tape is bounded.

options.text: The machine is forbidden from rereading input symbols
options.explanation: The machine may scan and rescan input while retaining small counters.

options.text: The input is compressed to a constant number of bits

workedExample:
1. The input is already available to read.
2. Count only scratch memory allocated by the computation.
3. A few positions or counters can then use logarithmic space even when the input itself is large.
